name: Bagirmi Sultanate
summary: A Muslim kingdom south-east of Lake Chad, often paying tribute to Kanem-Bornu or Wadai; it became a French protectorate in 1897.

location.value: Along the Chari River south-east of Lake Chad, in today’s Chad, with its capital at Massenya.

terrain.value: Flat savanna and floodplains along the Chari and Logone rivers.

climate.value: Sahel and savanna: hot, with a summer rainy season and a long dry season.

resources.value: Sorghum and millet, fish from the rivers, cattle, and captives taken in raids.

disasters.value: Droughts and famines; invasions that burned Massenya.

population.value: Uncertain; 19th-century visitors gave very different figures.

urbanisation.value: Mostly villages; a royal capital and market towns.

disease.value: Malaria and other tropical diseases; smallpox outbreaks.

migration.value: Barma people formed the core; captives from the south were brought in by raids.

economicBase.value: Farming, fishing, and raiding southern peoples for captives sold north.

tradeRoutes.value: Trade north to Bornu and Wadai and on to the trans-Saharan routes; captives, ivory and cloth were traded.

wealth.value: Mostly from tribute and slave raiding.

moneyAndTax.value: Tribute, market taxes and trade goods; cowrie shells in many markets.

inequality.value: Rulers and nobles above free farmers; enslaved people at the bottom.

governmentType.value: A sultanate ruled by the Mbang, with court officials and provincial chiefs.

keyRulers.value: Mbang Abd Allah (about 1561–1602), who made Islam the court religion; Mbang Gaourang II, who accepted French protection (1897).

succession.value: Within the royal dynasty, often disputed between royal brothers and sons.

institutions.value: The Mbang’s court with titled officials, and Muslim scholars and judges.

stability.value: Often a vassal of Bornu and later of Wadai; invaded several times in the 1800s.

eliteConflict.value: Royal rivals sometimes asked Wadai or Bornu for help to take the throne.

armyAndTech.value: Armoured cavalry with lances and quilted horse armour; few firearms until the late 1800s.

majorWars.value: Wadai sacked Massenya (1871); Rabih az-Zubayr attacked and burned it again (1893).

territoryChange.value: Its core changed little, but it was squeezed between Bornu, Wadai and later Rabih and the French.

alliancesRivals.value: Paid tribute to Bornu and later to Wadai; allied with the French against Rabih in the 1890s.

scienceEducation.value: Oral learning; Qur’anic schools where Islam spread.

openness.value: Open to trade and to Muslim scholars; European travellers Heinrich Barth (1852) and Gustav Nachtigal (1872) visited.

communicationTransport.value: Footpaths, horses, boats on the Chari River and messengers.

religion.value: Islam at the court from about 1600, alongside older local beliefs among many subjects.

languageWriting.value: Bagirmi (Tar Barma), a Nilo-Saharan language; Arabic for religion and letters.

artsArchitecture.value: Mud-brick palaces and mosques at Massenya; woven cloth and leather work.

socialStructure.value: The royal clan and nobles, Muslim scholars, free farmers, and enslaved captives.

sharedIdentity.value: Barma identity and loyalty to the Mbang.

dailyLife.value: Most people farmed millet and sorghum, fished and lived in round thatched houses.

neighbours.value: Kanem-Bornu to the west, Wadai to the east, and non-Muslim peoples to the south.

ideasReligions.value: Islam spread from the court outward, linking Bagirmi to scholars in Bornu and beyond.

colonisation.value: Mbang Gaourang II accepted a French protectorate (1897); later part of French Chad.

riseSignals.value: Founded around 1522 by Barma leaders near Massenya.

peakPeriod.value: Around 1600, under Mbang Abd Allah, when Bagirmi expanded and adopted Islam.

declineSignals.value: Wadai sacked Massenya (1871) and Rabih az-Zubayr devastated it (1893).

outcome.value: Became a French protectorate (1897) and part of the colony of Chad.

overallCertainty.value: Known from oral traditions, travellers and colonial records; many dates are approximate.
